newsitem.title: USA: No rating impact from Ohio school funding ruling.
newsitem.headline: No rating impact from Ohio school funding ruling.

text.p: An Ohio Supreme Court ruling that found the state's system of funding education to be unconstitutional will not lead to any immediate rating changes, according to analysts from the rating agencies.

Mike Forrester, a director at Standard & Poor's Corp., said Tuesday the agency would be looking to see what kind of plan lawmakers devise to replace the current system and how the new system would be funded.

He pointed out the state, which is rated AA-plus with a stable outlook, has a strong economy and some flexibility. He added that a new funding system could potentially help some low-wealth districts improve their bond ratings due to additional funding that may become available.

Richard Raphael, executive managing director at Fitch Investors Service, which rates Ohio AA-plus, said the agency would have to review the court's opinion and discuss its ramifications with state officials.
"(The state does) have a year to come up with a plan," he said.

In it's 4 to 3 decision released Monday, the court ruled that the state's school funding system violates the Ohio Constitution, which the court said mandates a thorough and efficient system of common schools throughout the state.
The ruling states that all the facts documented in the case "lead to one inescapable conclusion -- Ohio's elementary and secondary public schools are neither thorough nor efficient."

Justices gave Ohio one year to overhaul the funding system, but made it clear they do not advocate a so-called "Robin Hood" approach that would siphon funds from richer districts for use in poorer districts. The ruling also rejected spending ceilings on affluent school districts.

On Monday, Moody's Investors Service said the ruling would have no immediate impact on the ratings on more than 115 local school districts with a total of more than $19 billion of outstanding debt or on the state's A1-rated school district enhancement program.

The Ohio Supreme Court ruled specific parts of the funding system unconstitutional, including provisions granting borrowing authority to school districts, emergency school assistance loans, the School Foundation Program, and an "underfunded" Classroom Facilities Act.

The state's basic aid to school forumal has no "real relation" to what actually costs to educate a pupil, according to the majority opinion. In fact, the court said it makes no adjustment for the relative wealth of districts and forces districts to seek mostly unsuccessful levy increases from voters or turn to state-sanctioned borrowing for operational needs.
"These loan programs...are nothing less than a clever disguise for the state's failure to raise revenue sufficient to discharge its constitutional obligations," the court said.
The opinion also held that funding disparities between the districts were caused by the system's "overreliance on the tax base of individual school districts."
As for capital improvements, the court found the funding system lacked sufficient funds to meet the needs of poorer school districts.
The ruling concluded a six-year court battle between a coalition of school districts and the state over school funding.

In a statement released Monday, Gov. George Voinovich and legislative leaders expressed disappointment with the ruling, but pointed out the state has taken steps since 1991 to address funding disparities between districts and make more money available for school buildings and technology improvements.
